evidence.claim: Silver Bullet self-positions as an orchestration layer that runs inside Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor sessions rather than replacing the host runtime — satisfying process_layer_above_host and plugin_skill_hook_packaging.

Silver Bullet ships 12 layers of hook-enforced gates (SessionStart reset, PreToolUse planning gates, completion audits, stop hooks, branch-finish readiness) that block progress before PR creation or release — a deterministic_gates claim, not advisory.
Silver Bullet exposes 22 pre-composed workflows built from 27 reusable atomic flows with 85 flow-step V-loops and evidence schemas, covering feature, bugfix, UI, DevOps, deploy, canary and release.
Silver Bullet uses a two-tier delivery discipline: intermediate commits require only the planning floor, while final delivery (PR/release/deploy) requires full verification evidence.
Silver Bullet is free and open-source (Ālo Labs alpha) with no telemetry or lock-in, placing it at price parity with OSS methodology packs rather than with SaaS peers.
BMAD-METHOD is MIT-licensed, bring-your-own-model, and had approached ~49k GitHub stars — the highest-distribution OSS substitute in the secondary market.

BMAD structures delivery around 12–21 specialist agent personas (Analyst, PM, Architect, Scrum Master, Dev, QA/Test Architect, UX) with explicit deliverables and structured handoffs — strong specialist_agents score.
BMAD's two-phase model (agentic planning, then context-engineered implementation) produces complete specs before code, spanning plan→build→test — satisfies lifecycle_span.
BMAD installs into Claude Code and Cursor via a single command (npx bmad-method install), meeting plugin_skill_hook_packaging.
BMAD's enforcement is prompt/persona-level rather than hook-level; no machine-checkable stop-gate is documented, so it scores lower than Silver Bullet on deterministic_gates.

GitHub Spec Kit is MIT-licensed and describes itself as an extensible, intent-driven harness that pushes any coding agent beyond code, across the SDLC — direct process_layer_above_host positioning from a first-party vendor.

Spec Kit introduces constitution.md as a set of non-negotiable project principles enforced across phases — the closest OSS analogue to a policy layer, though enforcement is agent-interpreted rather than hook-blocked.

Spec Kit supports 29+ named agent integrations plus a generic adapter (Claude Code, Copilot, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Codex CLI, Windsurf, Goose, Roo Code and others) — the broadest host portability in the comparison set.
Spec Kit's persistent spec artifacts serve as the cross-session state mechanism (specification as source of truth) rather than a runtime state machine.

Superpowers (Jesse Vincent / obra) installs a composable skills framework into Claude Code covering brainstorming, design, plan-writing, TDD, systematic debugging, subagent-driven development with built-in code review, and skill authoring — multi-phase lifecycle_span in plugin packaging.

Superpowers enforces a red-green-refactor discipline in which tests must fail before implementation is written, and decomposes approved plans into 2–5 minute tasks with exact file paths and verification steps.
Superpowers is distributed through the first-party Claude plugin directory, giving it the lowest-friction install path among secondary-market substitutes.

Reported Superpowers star counts in secondary sources (~248k) are implausible for a Claude Code plugin and should be treated as unverified; use the GitHub repo as the authoritative counter before publishing any adoption figure.
Ruflo (formerly Claude Flow, by ruvnet) packages the SPARC methodology — Specification, Pseudocode, Architecture, Refinement, Completion — as a test-driven process layer over Claude Code.

Ruflo uses a hive-mind topology (queen agent coordinating specialised sub-agents) with 4 swarm topologies and 87 MCP tools, and was rewritten in Rust with persistent memory and MCP bridging — strong specialist_agents and cross_session_state scores.

AWS AI-DLC is an open-source methodology (published July 2025; awslabs/aidlc-workflows open-sourced November 2025) structured as Inception → Construction → Operations 'bolts' with mandatory human validation at each step.

AI-DLC's core principle is AI-powered execution with human oversight — agents draft plans, code, tests and infrastructure while deferring critical decisions to humans, matching the APO compliance-wrapper pattern.

AWS-reported AI-DLC outcomes (6 engineers, 100k lines of production Rust in 76 days; 4.5x developer velocity at Amazon Stores) are vendor-published and uncontrolled — cite as vendor claim, not benchmark.

'Conductor' is an ambiguous name across at least four distinct products (conductor.build Mac app, microsoft/conductor CLI, ryanmac/code-conductor, Conductor OSS); solution cards must disambiguate by vendor and URL.

Conductor (conductor.build) runs multiple Claude Code and Codex agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree, with a visual dashboard and diff-first review; it is free with BYO API cost and targets 3–8 parallel features per repo.

microsoft/conductor is MIT-licensed and provides deterministic YAML-defined routing with parallel groups and configurable failure modes (fail_fast, continue_on_error, all_or_nothing) over the Copilot SDK and Anthropic Agents SDK — the strongest deterministic_gates evidence among APO peers besides Silver Bullet.

Factory.ai repositioned from coding agents to 'software factories' and reached GA with Droids spanning the entire SDLC — code, knowledge/technical-writing, and reliability (SRE incident response) personas.

Factory's Droids handle end-to-end delivery — writing code, running tests, reviewing PRs, and pushing deployments — in production at NVIDIA, EY, Adobe, Palo Alto Networks, Adyen, Blackstone, Wipro and Comarch.
Factory closed a $150M Series C at a $1.5B valuation (Khosla Ventures and Sequoia leading), following a $50M round in September 2025 — high viability, high displacement risk in enterprise segments.

Augment Cosmos self-describes as 'the operating system for agentic software development', with agents running in the customer env or Augment cloud across the SDLC and humans steering where judgment matters.

Cosmos coordinates agents across triage, authoring, review and verification with shared team memory and self-improving loops, multi-model by default — direct functional overlap with APO cross_session_state and specialist_agents.

Cosmos entered public preview around May–June 2026 and is gated to the MAX plan at $200/developer/month or custom Enterprise pricing — a ~$2,400/dev/year floor versus $0 for Silver Bullet and the OSS packs.
Product-level naming requires listing 'Augment Cosmos' (not Augment Code, which is a hard exclusion as the parent coding-agent product) and 'Devin' (not Cognition).

Devin plans, writes, tests, ships, debugs, deploys and monitors inside sandboxed environments with shell, browser, editor and multiple sub-agents — full lifecycle_span but as a host runtime, not a layer above one.
Devin's July 2026 pricing spans Free, Pro $20/seat/mo, Max $200/seat/mo, Teams $80/mo base + $40/full dev seat, and custom Enterprise — the widest price ladder in the tertiary market.

Cognition raised over $1B at a $26B post-money valuation on 27 May 2026 (up from $10.2B eight months earlier) and partnered with Cognizant to scale autonomous software engineering into enterprise operations.

Tembo delegates work to Claude Code, Cursor and Codex across repos, triggered from Slack, Linear, GitHub and Sentry — a managed orchestration layer above host runtimes, qualifying it as a tertiary-market APO substitute despite no APO self-label.

Tembo enforces a human approval gate so nothing merges unreviewed, runs each agent in an isolated cloud VM preloaded with repo and dependencies, supports self-hosted VPC deployment, and claims no single-agent/model lock-in.

Tembo's last disclosed round was a $14M Series A (July 2024) after pivoting from managed Postgres; it is materially under-capitalised versus Factory ($1.5B) and Cognition ($26B), making it the most fragile tertiary entrant on a startup-weighted viability axis.

Zuvo could not be corroborated by open web search in this retrieval pass; its OSS license status is asserted by the category pack and must be verified against a primary repo/license file before the solution card asserts licensing.

The secondary market splits cleanly on enforcement mechanism: Silver Bullet and microsoft/conductor use machine-checkable blocking gates, while BMAD, Spec Kit, Superpowers and Ruflo rely on prompt-, artifact-, or persona-level discipline that an agent can in principle skip.

The tertiary SaaS market competes on managed infrastructure and enterprise distribution rather than on host-integrated process enforcement, so it substitutes for APO on outcome (shipped software with review gates) rather than on architecture.

Academic framing of agentic software engineering identifies verification and enforcement as foundational pillars, supporting the market thesis that a gate-enforcing process layer is a durable category rather than a transient wrapper.

Startup-weighted scoring favours the OSS secondary market on cost ($0 vs $200/dev/mo for Cosmos and Devin Max) and on absence of vendor lock-in, but favours the tertiary SaaS market on managed infrastructure and support burden.

claim_candidates.text: The APO (Agentic Process Orchestrator) category is best defined by a compliance/enforcement layer sitting above a host coding-agent runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor), rather than by autonomous code generation capability; Silver Bullet self-positions this way via hooks, skills, and a branch-scoped state machine.

Silver Bullet's differentiating mechanism versus secondary-market methodology packs is deterministic, machine-checkable gating: PreToolUse/Stop hooks that block commits, PR creation, and release when required skills have not been recorded in state — as opposed to prompt-level guidance that an agent may ignore.

Secondary-market OSS methodology packs (BMAD-METHOD, GSD, Superpowers, GitHub Spec Kit, SuperClaude, Ruflo/Claude Flow, Oh My Pi, Zuvo) satisfy lifecycle_span, plugin_skill_hook_packaging, and specialist_agents, but most satisfy deterministic_gates only partially — they are the most credible functional substitutes for Silver Bullet on adoption cost and community distribution.

GitHub Spec Kit is the strongest institutional threat in the secondary market because it is vendor-backed (GitHub) and establishes spec-driven development as a default convention, which commoditizes the plan/spec phase that APO products otherwise monetize.

Tertiary-market agentic SDLC SaaS (Factory.ai, Devin, Augment Cosmos, Tembo) do not self-label as process orchestrators but qualify as analyst-grade substitutes because they bundle lifecycle_span, cross_session_state, and specialist_agents inside a proprietary runtime — they compete for the same buyer budget while failing process_layer_above_host.

Factory.ai is the closest tertiary-market analogue to APO positioning because it markets 'Droids' as role-specialized agents governed by organizational process and enterprise controls, which maps to specialist_agents plus quality_release_enforcement.
Zuvo should be classified as OSS-licensed within the secondary market, not commercial; misclassifying it as commercial overstates the paid-substitute density of the SDLC-plugins market.

The primary APO market is structurally immature: most named seeds (Turboshovel, Cavekit v3.1, Barkain Workflow Orchestrator, cc10x, Director, AgentHub, ATeam, Claude Harness) are single-maintainer OSS packs without pricing, SLAs, or enterprise governance, meaning competition is on process depth and host-compatibility rather than commercial moat.

AI-DLC is a methodology/framework rather than a shipped host-integrated product; it should appear in the APO market chart as a low-packaging, high-lifecycle-span outlier that shapes buyer vocabulary without being directly substitutable.

Conductor occupies a distinct sub-position — parallel-worker orchestration and workspace isolation for coding agents — making it complementary rather than substitutive to gate-enforcement APOs like Silver Bullet.

For a startup-weighted comparison matrix, the highest-weight dimensions are adoption friction (install-to-first-gate time), host portability (Claude Code / Codex / Cursor coverage), and gate determinism; enterprise procurement dimensions (SOC2, SSO, audit export) are low-weight in primary and secondary markets but decisive in the tertiary market.

Cross-session state persistence is the most under-served inclusion criterion across the secondary market: most methodology packs rely on markdown artifacts re-read per session rather than an enforced state machine keyed to branch or worktree identity.

## Category market contract — Agentic SDLC Process Orchestrators

**Definition:** Systems that add repeatable workflows, cross-session state, deterministic quality gates, specialist agents, and enforcement above the host coding-agent runtime — not generic AI coding assistants, foundation-model labs, or single-step SDLC tools. Closest comps orchestrate full or multi-phase software delivery and DevOps cycles as composable, host-integrated process layers (plugins, skills, hooks).

**Jobs to be done:**
- Enforce a full SDLC or DevOps cycle so agents cannot skip planning, verification, review, or release steps
- Compose specialist agents and external workflows (GSD, spec kits, review ladders) under one compliance layer
- Persist process state, gates, and evidence across sessions and parallel workers
- Provide procurement-ready comparison of process-orchestration depth vs host runtimes and frameworks

**Inclusion criteria (candidate must pass ≥3 of 7):**
  - **lifecycle_span** (Multi-phase lifecycle span): Covers two or more of plan/spec, build, test, review, release, or DevOps operations as an integrated process — not a single-shot codegen or review-only tool.
  - **plugin_skill_hook_packaging** (Plugin / skill / hook packaging): Ships as host-integrated packaging (Claude/Codex/Cursor plugin, skill bundle, hook layer, or equivalent) rather than a standalone IDE or raw API.
  - **deterministic_gates** (Deterministic quality gates): Uses machine-checkable gates (hooks, audits, stop-checks, CI integration) that block progression when criteria fail.
  - **cross_session_state** (Cross-session state): Persists workflow state, memory, or runbooks across agent clears, sessions, or parallel workers.
  - **specialist_agents** (Specialist agent orchestration): Routes work to named specialist agents, hats, or role-specific subagents — not a single monolithic agent.
  - **quality_release_enforcement** (Quality / release enforcement claim): Publicly claims enforcement of quality, compliance, release, or governance — not advisory-only suggestions.
  - **process_layer_above_host** (Process layer above host runtime): Positions as a meta-orchestrator or compliance wrapper above Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or similar — not as the host runtime itself.

**Exclusion classes (never Top-N / MQ / Wave / matrix — Adjacent or Excluded only):**
  - `coding_agent` — Generic AI coding agent: IDE copilots, autocomplete agents, and autonomous SWE bots whose primary job is writing code — not enforcing a full process lattice.
  - `host_runtime` — Host runtime: The underlying agent host (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, Copilot) when evaluated as the runtime itself — adjacent only, not a process-orchestrator peer.
  - `single_sdlc_step` — Single SDLC step tool: Point solutions for one step only: code review bots, test generators, security scanners, design tools without workflow orchestration.
  - `generic_agent_framework` — Generic agent framework: Reusable multi-agent libraries (LangGraph, CrewAI, MetaGPT) without a shipped, enforced SDLC process product.
  - `project_management` — Project management: Issue trackers and PM SaaS (Linear, Jira-style) without agentic process enforcement.
  - `foundation_model_lab` — Foundation model lab: Model providers and research labs — not process-orchestration products.
  - `sunset` — Sunset / discontinued: Products officially discontinued or abandoned; never list in Top-N, charts, or matrix.

Claiming SB 'satisfies all 7 inclusion criteria' at 0.92 confidence is unsupported without public evidence for criteria 6 (quality/release enforcement claim). The claim cites sb.alolabs.dev but this is the product's own site — not independent validation. The 'most complete open-source APO' superlative needs comparative evidence (how many criteria does each competitor satisfy?). Suggestion: add a scored criteria matrix before making superlative claims.

critiques.target: Secondary market underweighted in competitive threat assessment
critiques.finding: The analysis correctly identifies SDLC plugins as 'the most formidable substitute set' but the solution-card depth planned for secondary market appears lighter than for APO. BMAD, GSD, and Superpowers each have distinct design philosophies (methodology-first vs. workflow-first vs. prompt-pack-first) that deserve the same criteria-based comparison as APO seeds. Suggestion: apply the same 7-criteria scoring to secondary-market products so the 'formidable substitute' claim is evidence-based.

Several established process-orchestration platforms are absent from the must-research list: (1) Dify.ai — visual workflow builder with multi-agent orchestration, gated pipelines, and cross-session state; satisfies ≥4 inclusion criteria. (2) Fixie.ai — agent orchestration platform with deterministic routing and plugin packaging. (3) LangGraph Platform / LangSmith — the LangChain ecosystem ships actual SDLC-process enforcement via LangGraph's human-in-the-loop and LangSmith's evaluation gates. Even though LangGraph is listed as 'generic_agent_framework,' the LangSmith evaluation layer satisfies deterministic_gates and quality_release_enforcement. Suggestion: add Dify.ai and LangSmith to must-research; evaluate against inclusion criteria rather than excluding by product-line ancestry.

The inclusion criteria specify ≥3 of 7 to pass, but there is no rubric for HOW each criterion is evaluated (binary, Likert, weighted). Without a documented scoring methodology, comparisons are opaque and unverifiable. Different evaluators could score the same product differently. Suggestion: define a 0-3 scale per criterion with anchor examples, and include a scored matrix as a figure/chart.

Factory.ai, Devin, Augment Cosmos, and Tembo are listed but there's no evidence of product-specific research into their actual process-orchestration layers. Factory.ai's 'Factory OS' is a test/CI orchestration platform that may satisfy deterministic_gates and lifecycle_span — but this needs source-backed investigation. Without it, the tertiary analysis risks being name-only. Suggestion: conduct product-level research for each tertiary seed before charting.

gaps.description: No TAM/SAM/SOM estimates exist for any of the three markets. The procurement audience needs market size context to evaluate investment relevance. Even rough ranges (e.g., 'APO TAM estimated at $X00M by 2027 based on Y reports') would anchor the landscape.
gaps.suggested_action: Research analyst reports (Gartner, Forrester) or VC funding data to estimate market size ranges per segment. If no public estimates exist, derive from adjacent markets (agent orchestration platforms, DevOps toolchains).

gaps.description: The analysis has no pricing data. For a procurement-targeted landscape, pricing tiers (free, pro, enterprise, self-hosted) are table stakes. Missing pricing makes the 'substitute set' analysis incomplete — a free OSS pack may be a better substitute than a $50/seat SaaS even if functionally weaker.
gaps.suggested_action: Research and add a pricing dimension to the comparison matrix: open-source (free), freemium, per-seat SaaS, self-hosted enterprise. Annotate where pricing is undisclosed.

gaps.description: No assessment of code quality, extensibility architecture, performance characteristics, or security posture. These matter for enterprise procurement (vendor risk, maintainability, security audit).

gaps.description: The landscape lacks a 'best fit for scenario' analysis. Different APOs suit different use cases (compliance-heavy enterprise vs. fast-prototyping solo dev). Without this, the landscape is just a list rather than actionable guidance.

gaps.description: No consideration of regional differences in APO adoption, regulatory constraints (EU AI Act, data sovereignty), or language support. A landscape that ignores geography may miss important procurement factors.
